section: What happens when articaine is injected into a nerve?
sentence_as_it_stands: The finding still stands. Twenty-nine papers have cited it in the fifteen years since. **None of them contradicts it**, and the paper carries no retraction, correction or expression of concern.
quote: So, it was suggested that an important cause of paresthesia could be related to the local anesthetic dosedependent neurotoxicity. Some in vitro studies support this hypothesis [27,28]. … the hypothesis that this local anesthetic may be neurotoxic was not confirmed in the present study.
corrected_wording: At least one citing paper reaches the opposite conclusion from a different design: Baroni 2013, the study set beside Hillerup in the next paragraph, cites it as support for the neurotoxicity hypothesis and concludes that articaine is not toxic to nerve structure, after an injection beside rather than into the mental nerve examined at 24 hours; it does not test Hillerup's intraneural measurement.
notes: Same point as claim update C050 (own question); adds the page location. Baroni is one of the citing papers (ref 28, cited once, PDF p5), but the page introduces it in the next paragraph as 'One other animal study' without registering that it cites Hillerup. The corrected wording replaces only 'None of them contradicts it'; the citation count and the retraction status are not examined here. The Sources entry ('none is classified as contrasting or contradicting') is consistent with Baroni's own citation sentence, which presents Hillerup as support; the main-text sentence goes further. Graded low as over-broad wording: the page already sets Baroni beside Hillerup, and Baroni's design does not test the intraneural finding the recommendation rests on; the main session may raise it because the sentence sits on the page's central safety argument.

section: What happens when articaine is injected into a nerve?
sentence_as_it_stands: Baroni and colleagues (2012) injected [dose figure omitted] articaine with epinephrine, [dose figure omitted] lidocaine with epinephrine, or **epinephrine alone** into the anterior portion of the mental nerve in 24 rats, with saline on the opposite side as the comparison, and examined the tissue under a microscope 24 hours later.
quote: The previous described solutions ([dose figure omitted]) were injected in the alveolar mucosa close to the lowerright first molar of rats (Figure 1)
corrected_wording: Baroni and colleagues (2013) injected articaine with epinephrine, lidocaine with epinephrine, or epinephrine alone into the mucosa beside the lower first molar, near the mental nerve rather than into it, in 24 rats, with saline on the opposite side as the comparison, and examined the tissue under a microscope 24 hours later.
notes: The wording follows Baroni's abstract ('injected in the anterior portion of mental nerve'), which reads as an injection into the nerve; the Methods and Figure 1 (PDF p3) place it in the alveolar mucosa near the nerve. The page contradicts itself: the next paragraph says 'Baroni injected into the region of a nerve, while Hillerup injected inside one', and the Sources entry's limits say 'injection into the region of the nerve rather than inside it', while the same Sources entry repeats the abstract wording ('injected into the anterior portion of the mental nerve') - second place. The extraneural route is what lets the page say the two studies do not collide, and what the practical step 'the evidence of harm comes entirely from drug delivered inside a nerve sheath' relies on.

section: What happens when articaine is injected into a nerve?
sentence_as_it_stands: The epinephrine result is the finding in Baroni with the most direct bearing on a self-administered wheal, and it does not favour adding a vasoconstrictor.
quote: The most intense inflammatory infiltration was observed when epinephrine was administered without local anesthetic (Group 3). This could be explained by the most intense vasoconstriction in the connective tissue, causing a more expressive hypoxia. … in the present study no significant increase in score inflammation was observed 24 h after articaine injection.
corrected_wording: The epinephrine result in Baroni is that epinephrine injected without an anaesthetic produced more inflammation at 24 hours than either anaesthetic-with-epinephrine solution, and neither of those differed significantly from saline; the study had no anaesthetic-without-epinephrine arm, so it does not compare an anaesthetic with and without a vasoconstrictor.
notes: Both anaesthetic arms contained the same epinephrine as the epinephrine-alone arm (PDF p3), and the authors attribute the lower inflammation in those arms to the anaesthetics' vasodilation offsetting epinephrine's vasoconstriction (PDF p5). Lidocaine with epinephrine was 'similar to saline solution' (PDF p5). Second place: practical step 4 uses the same finding as a reason (next finding; claim C062).

section: What does all of this mean for a wheal? (practical steps, item 4)
sentence_as_it_stands: It halves the vasoconstrictor for the same articaine, and the only animal study to inject epinephrine alone found it produced more tissue inflammation than either anesthetic did.
quote: The groups were represented by: Group 1, articaine [dose figure omitted] with epinephrine [dose figure omitted]; Group 2, lidocaine [dose figure omitted] with epinephrine [dose figure omitted]; and Group 3, solution of epinephrine [dose figure omitted].
corrected_wording: One animal study injected epinephrine alone beside a nerve in the jaw (Baroni 2013, rats): it found more connective-tissue inflammation at 24 hours than with either anaesthetic-with-epinephrine solution, neither of which differed significantly from saline; all its epinephrine-containing arms used the same epinephrine concentration, so it compared no epinephrine concentrations. Rat intrathecal studies with an epinephrine-alone arm found no histological change compared with saline (Hashimoto 2001, Komatsu 2013).
notes: The step gives two reasons for its preference between epinephrine presentations; this one does not test that preference: Baroni's epinephrine-alone arm had no anaesthetic, its two anaesthetic arms carried the same epinephrine and did not differ significantly from saline (PDF p5), and no arm used another epinephrine concentration or an anaesthetic without epinephrine. The step's first sentence (the preference itself, with its figures) is not copied. Overlaps claim update C062 (uniqueness already refuted on Hashimoto 2001 and Komatsu 2013) and finding F03.

section: Sources — Damage to nerve tissue (Baroni entry)
sentence_as_it_stands: Effect of articaine on mental nerve anterior portion: histological analysis in rats. *Acta Odontologica Scandinavica* 2012;71(1):82–7. PMID 22458536. DOI 10.3109/00016357.2011.654243.
corrected_wording: Effect of articaine on mental nerve anterior portion: histological analysis in rats. Acta Odontologica Scandinavica 2013;71(1):82–7 (published online 2012). PMID 22458536. DOI 10.3109/00016357.2011.654243.
notes: 2012 is the online-first year (PubMed: epub 29 March 2012); volume 71, issue 1 is the January 2013 print issue, as the PDF header shows. The main text also says 'Baroni and colleagues (2012)'. PMID and DOI are correct, so the paper is unambiguous.

section: Sources — Nerve damage in the laboratory (Radwan entry); closing note on entries resting on abstracts
sentence_as_it_stands: **Radwan IAM, Saito S, Goto F.** The neurotoxicity of local anesthetics on growing neurons: a comparative study of lidocaine, bupivacaine, mepivacaine, and ropivacaine. *Anesthesia and Analgesia* 2002. — The chick-neuron assay placing mepivacaine about [dose figure omitted] gentler than the other three. Limits: growing embryonic neurons in culture.
quote: we performed in vitro cell biological experiments with isolated dorsal root ganglion neurons from chick embryos. The effects of lidocaine, bupivacaine, mepivacaine, and ropivacaine were examined microscopically and quantitatively assessed using the growth cone collapse assay.
corrected_wording: Radwan IAM, Saito S, Goto F. The neurotoxicity of local anesthetics on growing neurons: a comparative study of lidocaine, bupivacaine, mepivacaine, and ropivacaine. Anesthesia and Analgesia 2002;94(2):319–24. PMID 11812691. DOI 10.1097/00000539-200202000-00016. — The chick-neuron assay placing mepivacaine about [dose figure omitted] gentler than the other three (checked against the PubMed record and abstract; full text not read). Limits: growing embryonic neurons in culture.
notes: Came from Baroni's reference list (ref 31; Baroni cites it for a prilocaine-versus-lidocaine rat finding it does not contain - that finding is Kishimoto 2002, which the prilocaine-wheals page attributes correctly). The page's closing note lists Radwan among entries that 'still rest on abstracts and citing papers' and asks for them to be verified before citing; the PubMed record confirms authors, title, journal and year and supplies the PMID and DOI, and the abstract supports the page's description (mepivacaine needed a markedly higher concentration than the other three for the same effect; the authors' conclusion favours mepivacaine). Verification is at abstract level only. This is a wheal page tested by another session: finding only.

page: 2 — Reference — Topical Treatments for Small Fiber Neuropathy
sentence_as_it_stands: **Articaine carries the field’s one clinical argument that concentration itself is neurotoxic.**
quote: Several authors [10–13] have reported that [dose figure omitted] solutions used in dentistry, articaine and prilocaine, are associated with paresthesia, mainly for inferior alveolar blocks.
corrected_wording: Articaine shares the field’s one clinical argument that concentration itself is neurotoxic with the other high-concentration dental solution, prilocaine: reports of persistent paraesthesia after dental blocks are over-represented for both.
notes: Ambiguous rather than plainly wrong: the paragraph continues with the Danish registry study, in which articaine was the only high-concentration product. Baroni's background (refs 10-13: Haas & Lennon 1995, Gaffen & Haas 2009, Garisto 2010, Hillerup & Jensen 2006) reports the signal for both the articaine and prilocaine dental solutions, and the record's own prilocaine-wheals page (as of 2026-10-02T03:14:12.541Z, section 'What does the evidence say about prilocaine irritating nerves?') says 'the [dose figure omitted] dental solution carries the strongest paresthesia signal of any local anesthetic'. The concentration argument rests on both drugs. The Reference has no entry for Baroni or Hillerup.

page: Comparing the injectable local anesthetics for intradermal wheals
section: What does each one do to nerve tissue?
sentence_as_it_stands: Injecting [dose figure omitted] articaine directly into a rat’s sciatic nerve left conduction measurably reduced three weeks later, with thinner fibers and thinner insulating sheaths; [dose figure omitted] did not produce those changes, and a needle plus salt water produced no effect at all (Hillerup et al., 2011).
quote: The evoked spinal cord field potential in the articaine groups faded away immediately after injection and was concentration-dependently, significantly more reduced at the 3-week follow-up in comparison with the saline group.
corrected_wording: Injecting articaine directly into a rat’s sciatic nerve left conduction reduced three weeks later in the articaine groups compared with salt water, more at the higher concentration; thinner fibers and thinner insulating sheaths were significant only at the higher concentration, and a needle plus salt water produced no effect at all (Hillerup et al., 2011).
notes: Came from Baroni's reference list (ref 28). Rests on the abstract only: it reports the three-week reduction for 'the articaine groups' against saline, concentration-dependently, and the fibre-area and myelin changes only for the higher concentration; it does not state the lower-concentration-versus-saline conduction test separately, so the full text should confirm (not reachable here: no PMC copy, and the Scite connector needs a paid plan). The record's articaine-wheals page reads the abstract the same way as this correction ('At three weeks, the response was still significantly more reduced than in the salt-water group, and the size of that reduction depended on concentration'), so the two pages disagree. Second place on this page: Sources, 'Damage to nerve tissue', Hillerup entry: 'Lasting conduction loss and structural change at [dose figure omitted] but not [dose figure omitted], with no effect from needle plus saline.'
